lessons.title: Projectiles
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board — Advanced Level Mathematics, Mechanics (Upper Sixth part; to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Resolve the initial velocity into horizontal and vertical components
Find time of flight, range and greatest height
reviewNotes: g=10 m/s² used (check whether the Board uses 9.8).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Model
blocks.md: Neglect air resistance. Horizontally the velocity is constant; vertically the acceleration is $g$ downwards ($g=10$ m/s² here). For launch speed $u$ at angle $\alpha$ above the horizontal: $u_x=u\cos\alpha$, $u_y=u\sin\alpha$.

blocks.title: Equations of motion
blocks.md: At time $t$: $x=u\cos\alpha\,t$, $y=u\sin\alpha\,t-\frac{1}{2}gt^2$; $v_x=u\cos\alpha$, $v_y=u\sin\alpha-gt$. Landing at the same level: time of flight $T=\frac{2u\sin\alpha}{g}$, range $R=\frac{u^2\sin2\alpha}{g}$, greatest height $H=\frac{u^2\sin^2\alpha}{2g}$ (when $v_y=0$).

blocks.title: Trajectory
blocks.md: Eliminating $t$: $y=x\tan\alpha-\frac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\alpha}$, a parabola. The speed at any time is $\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}$ and the angle with the horizontal is $\tan^{-1}\frac{|v_y|}{v_x}$.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- At the highest point the velocity is NOT zero: only the vertical component is.
- Use the vertical motion to find the time and then the horizontal motion for the distance.
- Do not use $R=\frac{u^2\sin2\alpha}{g}$ when the landing point is at a different height.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: A ball is hit from the ground at 20 m/s at $30\degree$ to the horizontal ($g=10$). Find the time of flight, the range and the greatest height.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: A stone is thrown horizontally at 12 m/s from a cliff 45 m high. How far from the base does it land?

lessons.title: Moments and equilibrium
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board — Advanced Level Mathematics, Mechanics (Upper Sixth part; to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Calculate the moment of a force about a point
Use the two conditions for equilibrium
Solve beam, seesaw and pivot problems
reviewNotes: Ladder and inclined-force problems (friction at wall and ground) not included; check if required.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Moment
blocks.md: The moment of a force $F$ about a point is $F\times d$, where $d$ is the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force. Unit: N m. Its sense is clockwise or anticlockwise.

blocks.title: Equilibrium of a rigid body
blocks.md: A body is in equilibrium when (1) the resultant force is zero (upward forces = downward forces) and (2) the total moment about any point is zero (clockwise = anticlockwise). Take moments about a point where an unknown force acts to remove it from the equation.

blocks.title: Method
blocks.md: 1. Draw a diagram with all forces (weight of a uniform beam acts at its midpoint). 2. Choose a point to take moments about. 3. Sum clockwise moments = sum anticlockwise moments. 4. Resolve vertically to find the other reaction. 5. Check that both reactions are positive (a negative reaction means the beam lifts off that support).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using the distance along the beam when the force is inclined: you need the PERPENDICULAR distance.
- Putting the weight at the end of a uniform beam instead of the middle.
- Forgetting the weight of the beam itself.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: A uniform beam $AB$ of length 4 m and weight 200 N rests on supports at its ends. A child of weight 300 N stands 1 m from $A$. Find the reactions at $A$ and $B$.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: A 40 kg child sits 1.5 m from the pivot of a seesaw. Where must a 30 kg child sit on the other side to balance it?

lessons.title: Work, energy, power and momentum
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board — Advanced Level Mathematics, Mechanics (Upper Sixth part; to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use work, kinetic and potential energy and the work-energy principle
Use conservation of momentum and impulse
reviewNotes: Coefficient of restitution and oblique impacts not included.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Energy and power
blocks.md: Work done by a constant force $=Fd$ (in the direction of the force), in joules. Kinetic energy $=\frac{1}{2}mv^2$; gravitational potential energy $=mgh$. Work-energy principle: work done by the resultant force $=$ change in kinetic energy. Power $=\frac{\text{work}}{\text{time}}=Fv$, in watts.

blocks.title: Momentum
blocks.md: Momentum $p=mv$ (kg m/s). **Conservation**: in a collision with no external force, total momentum before = total momentum after. Impulse $=Ft=$ change in momentum $=mv-mu$ (N s). Kinetic energy is NOT conserved in an inelastic collision (energy is lost as heat and sound).

blocks.title: Method
blocks.md: For motion under gravity without friction use $\frac{1}{2}mv^2+mgh=$ constant. With friction: work by friction $=$ friction force $\times$ distance reduces the energy. For collisions: choose a positive direction, write $m_1u_1+m_2u_2=m_1v_1+m_2v_2$, then compare kinetic energies if asked.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md: Momentum is a vector: a rebound reverses the sign (impulse on a ball bouncing off a wall is $m(v_1+v_2)$). Do not use $F=\frac{\Delta KE}{t}$ for power. Check units: J, W, N s.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: A 2 kg ball is dropped from 5 m ($g=10$). Find its speed on impact and its kinetic energy.
steps: $KE=\frac{1}{2}(2)(100)=100$ J (equal to the lost potential energy $2\times10\times5$).

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: A 3 kg trolley at 4 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg trolley and they stick together. Find the common speed and the kinetic energy lost.

lessons.title: Motion in a horizontal circle
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board — Advanced Level Mathematics, Mechanics (Upper Sixth part; to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use angular speed $\omega$, speed $v=r\omega$ and period
Use the centripetal acceleration $\frac{v^2}{r}$ and force $\frac{mv^2}{r}$
Solve problems with tension and friction
reviewNotes: Vertical circles and banked tracks not included.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Angular motion
blocks.md: A particle moving in a circle of radius $r$ with angular speed $\omega$ (rad/s): $v=r\omega$. The period $T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}$ and $\omega=2\pi f$ where $f$ is the frequency (rev/s). Convert revolutions per minute: $\omega=\text{rpm}\times\frac{2\pi}{60}$.

blocks.title: Acceleration towards the centre
blocks.md: Even at constant speed the velocity changes direction, so there is an acceleration $a=\frac{v^2}{r}=r\omega^2$ directed towards the centre. The resultant force towards the centre is $F=\frac{mv^2}{r}=mr\omega^2$ (provided by tension, friction, a reaction...). It is not an extra force.

blocks.title: Method
blocks.md: 1. Identify the real forces (tension, friction, weight, reaction) that point towards the centre. 2. Write $F_{towards\;centre}=\frac{mv^2}{r}$. 3. Resolve vertically when needed (balanced). 4. For a car on a flat bend friction gives $\mu mg\geq\frac{mv^2}{r}$, so the maximum speed satisfies $v^2=\mu gr$.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md: There is no 'centrifugal force' pushing outwards in the equation of motion. Uniform circular motion has acceleration (not zero). Use radians per second, not revolutions per minute, in $v=r\omega$.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: A 0.5 kg stone is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 0.8 m at 4 m/s on a light string. Find the acceleration and the tension.
steps: Tension provides the centripetal force: $T=ma=0.5\times20=10$ N.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: A car goes round a flat bend of radius 50 m. The coefficient of friction is 0.4. Find the maximum speed ($g=10$).

exercises.prompt: A uniform beam $AB$ of length 6 m and weight 240 N is supported at $A$ and at $C$, where $AC=4$ m. A load of 80 N hangs at $B$. Find the reactions at $A$ and $C$.
exercises.model: Moments about $A$: $R_C\times4=240\times3+80\times6=1200$, so $R_C=300$ N. Vertically $R_A+R_C=320$, so $R_A=20$ N (positive, so the beam does not lift).
exercises.explanation: Moments about $A$: $R_C\times4=240\times3+80\times6=1200$, so $R_C=300$ N. Vertically $R_A+R_C=320$, so $R_A=20$ N (positive, so the beam does not lift).
